blocks.title: Photoperiodism
blocks.text: Photoperiodism is the response to changes in day length that enables plants to adapt to seasonal changes in their environment. Simply, it is the response of plants to the length of day and night.

The effect of photoperiod was first studied in 1920 by Garner and Allard, who found that the tobacco plant flowers only after exposure to a series of short days. Tobacco naturally flowers under those conditions in autumn, but flowering could be induced artificially by exposing it to short days. With further study they classified flowering plants into long-day plants, which need long days to flower, short-day plants, which need short days, and day-neutral plants, which flower regardless of photoperiod. Later studies showed that it is really the length of the dark period that is critical: short-day plants are really long-night plants. If they are grown in short days but the long night is interrupted by a short period of light, flowering is prevented; and long-day plants will flower in short days if the long night is interrupted.

Phytochrome, a photoreceptor protein, exists in two forms, P660 and P730. P660 is the quiescent form; it absorbs red light at 660 nm and is converted to the active P730, which absorbs far-red light at 730 nm and is converted back to P660. In nature the P660 to P730 conversion takes place in daylight and the P730 to P660 conversion in the dark. The rate at which P730 reverts to P660 gives the plant a clock for measuring the duration of darkness.

Red light inhibits flowering in short-day plants but promotes it in long-day plants under the conditions in which they normally flower. This led to the hypothesis that the P730-P660 interconversion might be the plant's time regulator for flowering: P730, made from P660 by red light, would inhibit flowering in short-day plants and promote it in long-day plants. Because P730 accumulates by day and diminishes at night, a short-day plant could flower only if the night were long enough for most of its P730 to be inactivated, while a long-day plant would need enough P730 left at the end of the night to promote flowering. It is now generally agreed that the timing of flowering is not controlled entirely by this interconversion; the presence or absence of light and the lengths of the dark and light periods also matter. Once stimulated, the biological clock causes the production of the hormone florigen in the leaves, which travels through the phloem to the floral buds and initiates flowering.
